extracted.intended_audience: novelists, critics, and advanced students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the craft of the realist novel: how to create a convincing world, manage time and point of view, select and present facts, and control method so a novel achieves coherent meaning and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of the book-world with the larger world
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no perceptible horizon, no hard line between the life in the book and the life beyond it. The communication between the men and women of the story and the rest of the world is unchecked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to make characters seem to inhabit 'our world' rather than a small story-book world; give them obvious latitude of movement so readers can imagine their lives beyond the page. Example contrast: Tolstoy's open horizon vs the enclosed world of many story-books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of landscape and implied distance to create space
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere association of a picture with the thought of illimitable plains or a river that lies across a continent enlarges the impression of space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hint or associative detail can evoke vastness; you do not need exhaustive description to suggest an extending world — cultural/geographic associations (e.g., 'Russia' as extent) can supply the necessary imagination of distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate horizon/illumination for the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fables require an ample, impartial daylight opening in every direction; others need a drawn curtain of darkness to intensify inner consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your story benefits from an expansive, open world (Tolstoy) or a claustrophobic, intensified theatrical lighting (Dostoevsky's 'blaze of light' and 'curtain of darkness'), and keep that tonal choice consistent with your subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant characters freedom beyond the page (not mere multitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the mere multiplication of names and households that creates breadth, but giving characters such freedom, such an obvious latitude of movement in the open world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid thinking that many named characters alone will enlarge scope; instead, render them with autonomy and a sense of existence outside the immediate scenes so readers can extend their lives imaginatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on description to create reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Description has nothing to do with it; there is very little description in War and Peace, yet the sense of space is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume detailed descriptive inventory is necessary for 'realness.' Character behavior, consistent treatment, and suggestion can convey reality more effectively than exhaustive description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the form of time (not only chronology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of time is to be represented; it is something more than to represent its contents in their order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the passage of time by the build of the whole book — its 'hues and masses' — not by announcing elapsed years. Narrative shape must make the movement of time perceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render both continuous lapse and cyclical arc of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Time has two aspects: its uninterrupted lapse, and the cycle of which the chosen stretch is a segment (the rise and fall of a generation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure readers perceive both the steady accumulation of years and the larger generational curve that gives the story its sweep; even a relatively short span can suggest a great wheel if shaped properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray believable aging and constancy in characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Young men and women grow older, cease to be young, grow old, with the noiseless regularity of life; their mutability never hides their sameness, their consistency shows and endures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track subtle changes in gesture, thought, and demeanor that indicate the passage of years while keeping each character true to earlier-established core traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design/coherence: chapters must collocate for a reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The picture's moral is in its design; without design the scattered scenes will make no picture. Chapters must draw together and announce a reason for their collocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a clear design or purpose so the aggregation of scenes forms a single, intelligible effect or 'moral' rather than a collection of worthy episodes that fail to cohere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix subject and method during composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither his subject nor his method were fixed for him as he wrote; he ranged around material never deciding to what end he had amassed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early (and sustain) what the central subject and the method of treatment are; vacillation about intention will scatter energy and weaken overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wasting material that dilutes the main effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Great masses of that life are being wasted, turned to no account; the wasted life divides and weakens the effect of the picture created out of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cull or reshape episodes that do not serve the novel's chosen design; extraneous richness can ironically diminish the force of the primary theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and use facts so they announce the intended meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The facts have no validity in themselves, they are nothing until they have been used; the novelist selects the information he offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat facts as material to be shaped; include only those details that help produce the impression or argument the novel intends to make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing versus telling: the novelist's problem of 'narration'
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist must state, must narrate—his book is a series of assertions—but the art of fiction begins when he thinks of his story as something to be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance necessary narration with methods that allow the story to 'tell itself' through selected presentation, dramatization, or pictorial rendering rather than mere report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic (immediate) vs panoramic (sweeping) presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are we placed before a particular scene at a certain hour? Or are we surveying lives from a height, sweeping their history with a wide range of vision?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether to render concentrated scenes or wide-range panoramas (or how to transition between them). Mark and manage shifts so the reader's relation to the action remains clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice vs character-pointed voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the author is talking with his own voice, sometimes he is talking through one of the people in the book — in this book for the most part Emma herself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide when to let the authorial perspective intervene and when to present events in the terms of a character's mind; the difference affects tone, judgment, and reader alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intervention to supply necessary knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: There comes a juncture at which it is necessary for us to know more than we could have made out by simply looking and listening; Flaubert must intervene with his superior knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authorial commentary or summary to supply background, past facts, or the characters' inner life when the immediate scene cannot convey essential meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (mood/subjective) versus dramatic (stageable) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a pictorial manner of treating the matter and there is also a dramatic. A scene may be pictorial — bathed in the climate of a character's mood — and would lose its effect if staged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether scenes should function as interior impressions (pictorial) or as externalized action (dramatic); understand that some literary effects depend on pictorial subjective rendering rather than theatrical reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and label shifts of method and point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless we purposely keep an eye upon the writer's devices, marking them off as he turns from one to another, we hardly notice the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of changes in method (scene vs summary, authorial vs character voice, pictorial vs dramatic) and make transitions deliberate so they serve your design rather than confuse the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain characters' truthfulness/consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are never less than absolutely true to themselves; wherever we meet them, in peace or war, they are always the people we know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure behavior and development remain consistent with the nature the author has established, even as they change with time; inconsistent actions undercut credibility.
